sentences.text: The Mascarene parrot measured 35 cm in length with a wingspan of 211 mm, a tail length between 144 and 152 mm, a culmen of 32 to 36 mm, and a tarsus of 22 to 24 mm.

Stuffed specimens and older descriptions indicate the body was brown with a bluish head, while one account from 1674 described live birds as 'petit-gris,' a dark grey similar to a red squirrel, and another noted a dark blackish grey or brown hue; these two surviving specimens also differ significantly in their coloration.
The skull lacked a mandibular fenestra, featured a broadly oval mandibular symphysis with a flattened lower margin, and possessed a sharply angled downward symphysis.
Only two stuffed specimens of the Mascarene parrot exist today, located in Paris and Vienna.
The Mascarene parrot was the last endemic bird species to go extinct on Réunion, preceding the hoopoe starling which disappeared in the mid-19th century.

The bird was first mentioned by French traveler Sieur Dubois in his 1674 travelogue of Réunion, and Carl Linnaeus scientifically described it as Psittacus mascarinus in 1771, with the species name referencing the Mascarene Islands named after Portuguese discoverer Pedro Mascarenhas.
It was scientifically described in 1771, and the genus Mascarinus was later established by Lesson in 1831.
The IOC World Bird List emended the binomial name to M. mascarin in 2016 to align with Linnaean conventions.

In 1834, German zoologist Carl Wilhelm Hahn published an account of a live Mascarene parrot belonging to King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria, and the IUCN Red List accepts this 1834 Hahn account as the final mention of a live Mascarene parrot.
Because several specimens were kept in captivity, the Mascarene parrot was likely not a specialized feeder.
A 1705 description by Jean Feuilley suggests that Mascarene parrots fattened themselves seasonally.
X-ray comparisons show that subfossil bones of the Mascarene parrot were intermediate in measurements between modern specimens and the stuffed ones.

The genus Mascarinus is classified within the parent group Psittaculini, and a 2011 genetic study placed the Réunion Mascarene parrot among subspecies of the black parrot from Madagascar and nearby islands; the genus name Mascarinus prevailed, and when combined with the specific name mascarinus in 1891, it formed a tautonym.

The taxonomic placement of the Mascarene parrot is debated, with recent genetic studies favoring its grouping with Psittaculini parrots over vasa parrots, and its evolutionary affinities have been debated since the mid-19th century.
Early writers incorrectly claimed the parrot was found on Madagascar, leading Lesson to propose the synonym Mascarinus madagascariensis in 1831.
The Mascarene parrot was endemic to the island of Réunion in the western Indian Ocean, and the genus Mascarinus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
The Mascarene parrot is recorded as extinct in 1834, and the last known account of wild Mascarene parrots on Réunion dates to the 1770s.

The date and cause of extinction are unclear; while 1834 is the latest record, it is considered dubious, suggesting extinction likely occurred before 1800 or even earlier. It is suggested that the removal of the skull and mandible prior to Forbes' study may have distorted the shape of the head and nostrils in his illustrations. Hume proposed that the brown coloration of the Mascarene parrot is an artifact of aged taxidermy, but this hypothesis is debated by researchers like Joseph M. Forshaw. Another group of scientists acknowledged the finding but noted the sample might have been deteriorated and more tests were needed to resolve the issue completely.
